title: Hijacked Bitly Links Redirect Old Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump Posts
text:
Hijacked Bitly Links Redirect Old Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump Posts | LavX News Skip to content LavX News Open Source Open Source Security Open Source Apps Open Source Infrastructure Open Source AI Open Source Dev Tools Trends Regulation Business Startups Hardware Chips Laptops Smartphones Cloud DevOps Serverless Infrastructure Security Vulnerabilities Privacy Cybersecurity Dev Python Rust Mobile Backend Frontend AI Robotics LLMs Machine Learning Bookmarks Sign In English Sign In # Cybersecurity Hijacked Bitly Links Redirect Old Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump Posts
 Nov 16, 2026, 12:08 AM UTC • Lukas Brandt • 2 min read Share this article Save Advertisement Advertise on LavX News See options Old Bitly links embedded in past posts from Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump were hijacked, sending visitors to destinations the original posters did not choose. The incident shows how expired or reclaimed short links can undermine trust in years-old social media content.
 Old Bitly links in past social media posts from Burger King, McDonald’s and Donald Trump were hijacked, according to a report published Nov. 15. The affected links, once shared through the brands’ and Trump’s accounts, no longer point to their original destinations.
 What happened
 The hijacked URLs rely on Bitly, a link-shortening service that turns long web addresses into compact links for posts and messages. When control over a shortened link or its destination changes, anyone who clicks an old post can land on a page selected by a new owner rather than the person or company that published the original message.
 The report identifies Burger King, McDonald’s and Trump as the subjects of the compromised links. Specific technical details about how the attackers gained control of the links were not included in the available information.
 Why it matters
 Shortened links can outlive the campaigns, promotions and news cycles that produced them. A tweet or post may remain online for years, while the infrastructure behind its links changes hands, expires or becomes vulnerable to takeover. That gap creates a lasting security and reputation risk for public figures, companies and anyone who depends on short links in archived content.
 For readers, the problem blurs the line between a trusted account and the destination behind its links. A familiar brand or name can lend credibility to a post long after the link inside it stops serving its original purpose.
 Reducing the risk
 Organizations can limit exposure by auditing old posts that contain shortened URLs, reclaiming or disabling links they no longer control and monitoring redirects for unexpected changes. Branded short domains and direct links to owned pages can also reduce dependence on third-party shorteners for long-lived communications.
 The episode serves as a reminder that social media content carries risk beyond the moment of publication. Links need the same review and maintenance as the accounts that share them.
